claim: Keloharju, Linnainmaa and Nyberg ('Common Factors in Return Seasonalities', AQR-hosted December 2014 working-paper version of the Journal of Finance article) sort 17 Fama-French industry portfolios by their average return in the same calendar month over the prior 20 years and trade the top two and bottom two portfolios long-short; over January 1963-December 2011 the industry same-month strategy earns 0.70% per month (t-value = 3.79), and 0.59% (t = 3.11) excluding January, while the other-month sort earns -0.81% (t = -4.32). This is the un-shifted same-calendar-month sort (shift 0); the paper does not test a one-month front-running shift, ETFs, or costs.
market_and_period: 17 Fama-French US industry portfolios (value-weighted), monthly, January 1963-December 2011; same-month sort over the prior 20 years, long top 2 / short bottom 2.
applicability: Primary support that same-calendar-month return seasonality exists at industry level (the mechanism the front-running rule leans on): I_K2_Y5 mirrors the top-2 sort with a 5-year (not 20-year) average. Supports the long leg only indirectly, since the paper reports a long-short spread and this lane is long-only (short bottom-2 not traded).
limitations: 1963-2011 gross portfolio returns, no transaction costs; 20-year averaging vs. at most 5 years of ETF history here (data start 2016-01); shift 0, not the shift-1 front-running variant; industries are Fama-French portfolios, not investable ETFs; the effect may have decayed after publication (2014 working paper).
independent_replication: Journal of Finance 2016 version of the same paper (peer-reviewed); Heston and Sadka (2008) report seasonalities largely independent of industry effects, per the paper own footnote. No independent ETF-level replication found.
impact_on_spec: Grounds the frozen 23-ETF industry universe and the top-N/avg_years grid; no parameter chosen from results.

claim: Quantpedia's 'Front-Running Seasonality in US Stock Sectors' page (9 Select Sector SPDRs XLB/XLE/XLF/XLI/XLK/XLP/XLU/XLV/XLY, Nov 2000-Nov 2023 backtest with data through Sep 2024) tests holding 1 through 7 ETFs long-only, monthly rebalance, and reports holding TWO ETFs in long positions is the best-performing cut of the 'front-running' variant (score-window shifted forward by one month vs. the naive 'true seasonality' baseline, which is 'at best, comparable to those of the benchmark'). Short positions were tested but found ineffective and dropped. The page does NOT test finer industry ETFs, multi-year score averaging, or a wider universe.
quote: holding two ETFs in long positions
market_and_period: 9 Select Sector SPDR ETFs, Nov 2000-Nov 2023 backtest window, data through Sep 5 2024.
applicability: Parent rule for this iteration: the front-running (shift 1) top-N long-only sort is reused verbatim (make_sector_seasonality_fn) and only the universe is widened from 9 sector SPDRs to 23 industry ETFs; top-N grid {2,3,5} and avg_years {1,5} are the preregistered extension.
limitations: Quantpedia numeric tables are chart images, not machine-readable; sector SPDRs, not industry ETFs; author flags the strategy seasonality chart as possibly coincidental; no transaction-cost detail in text.
independent_replication: Allocate Smartly tested the country-ETF version and did not find it consistently effective over a longer horizon (source card below); no independent replication of the sector or industry-ETF version.
impact_on_spec: Grounds the frozen 23-ETF industry universe and the top-N/avg_years grid; no parameter chosen from results.

claim: Allocate Smartly independently extended Quantpedia's front-running seasonality mechanism (applied to 23 country ETFs / MSCI country indices, not US sectors) back to 1971 using ~30+ additional years of MSCI index data beyond the original author's sample, and found the strategy 'would not have been consistently effective over the long-term' in that extended pre-sample period; they explicitly state they 'will not be tracking this strategy on an ongoing basis' as a result, despite the in-sample cut reporting a Sharpe of 0.46 vs. a 0.38 benchmark (CAGR 13.2% vs 11.2%, max drawdown -59.1%).
quote: we will not be tracking this strategy on an ongoing basis
market_and_period: 23 country ETFs / MSCI country indices, extended sample back to 1971.
applicability: Negative evidence for the whole front-running-seasonality family, closest independent replication attempt found; motivates the two-stage decision (placebo beat fraction and the C2 combination gates) rather than accepting a good recent Sharpe alone.
limitations: Country ETFs and MSCI index data, not US industry ETFs; different sample; the -59.1% max drawdown is a caution regardless.
independent_replication: None found beyond this single Allocate Smartly test.
impact_on_spec: Grounds the frozen 23-ETF industry universe and the top-N/avg_years grid; no parameter chosen from results.

claim: Heston and Sadka (October 2006 working-paper version of the JFE 2008 article) find that stocks with relatively high (low) returns tend to have high (low) returns every year in the same calendar month, a pattern lasting up to 20 annual lags, superimposed on momentum/reversal; per the abstract the pattern is independent of size, industry, earnings announcements, dividends and fiscal year. Their own result is that the seasonality is not an industry effect, which differs from KLN's finding of significant industry-portfolio seasonalities.
quote: independent of size, industry, earnings announcements
market_and_period: US individual stocks (CRSP), same-calendar-month lags up to 20 years.
applicability: Second independent primary paper for the same-calendar-month mechanism; also a caution that the effect is about individual stocks, so industry-level extension is an assumption tested here.
limitations: Individual-stock cross-section, gross returns, no ETFs, no costs; working-paper (2006) version; says industry does not explain the pattern.
independent_replication: Published JFE 2008; KLN 2016 confirm stock-level seasonality independently.
impact_on_spec: Context for decay/placebo/combination design; no parameter chosen from results.

claim: Moskowitz and Grinblatt (Journal of Finance 1999) document a strong and prevalent momentum effect in industry components of stock returns: strategies that buy stocks from past winning industries and sell stocks from past losing industries are highly profitable even after controlling for size, book-to-market, individual-stock momentum and microstructure effects.
quote: industry momentum investment strategies, which buy stocks from past winning industries
market_and_period: US stocks grouped into 20 industries, 1963-1995, 1-12 month formation windows.
applicability: The shift-1 front-running score (last year same-month + 1) partly overlaps with short-horizon industry momentum, which is why the placebo draws shifts from {2..9} and excludes 10-12 (momentum-contaminated), and why the C2 increment is judged on Sharpe, not on level.
limitations: 1963-1995 sample, stock portfolios not ETFs; momentum is a competing explanation, not a test of front-running.
independent_replication: Widely replicated industry momentum evidence; no ETF-level front-running replication.
impact_on_spec: Context for decay/placebo/combination design; no parameter chosen from results.

claim: Aalto University research portal record of Keloharju, Linnainmaa and Nyberg, 'Return Seasonalities', Journal of Finance 71(4), 2016 (peer-reviewed, 126 Scopus citations at fetch): a strategy that selects stocks based on their historical same-calendar-month returns earns an average return of 13% per year; similar seasonalities are documented in anomalies, commodities and international stock market indices, and the seasonalities are tied to shared systematic factors.
quote: earns an average return of 13% per year
market_and_period: US stocks, anomaly portfolios, commodities, international indices; 1963-2011.
applicability: Confirms the AQR working paper used above was published peer-reviewed (JF 2016); supports the seasonality mechanism at index/anomaly level.
limitations: Abstract-level record; strategies are long-short and gross of costs.
independent_replication: Peer-reviewed journal version of the AQR working paper.
impact_on_spec: Context for decay/placebo/combination design; no parameter chosen from results.

claim: Allocate Smartly (2024-12-20) independently tested Quantpedia's front-running commodity seasonality on 4 commodity ETFs (DBA, DBB, DBC, DBP), more than doubling the author's test length with index data since 1990, ignoring transaction and shorting costs (proof of concept): it notes a big run-up from 2000 to 2010 and that results outside that period have been essentially flat, and that the run-up survives a risk-parity version.
quote: Results outside of that period have been essentially flat
applicability: Second independent third-party test of the front-running family (commodity version) with regime-dependent outcome: evidence for decay-risk and for judging by the placebo, stress window and C2 increment instead of the recent Sharpe alone.
limitations: Commodity ETFs, long-short proof of concept without costs; not industry equities.
independent_replication: Independent of Quantpedia; no industry-ETF version tested.
impact_on_spec: Context for decay/placebo/combination design; no parameter chosen from results.

claim: McLean and Pontiff (October 2012 working-paper version of the JF 2016 article) study 82 published return predictors and find that the average post-publication decay, attributed to both statistical bias and price pressure from aware investors, is about 35%, and that after publication anomaly portfolios show higher volume, variance, short interest and correlation with other published anomaly portfolios.
quote: The average post-publication decay, which we attribute to both statistical bias and price pressure from aware investors, is about 35%
market_and_period: 82 US stock characteristics, in-sample vs post-publication periods.
applicability: Decay prior for a 2014-2016 published seasonality (KLN) now traded through 2024-2026: expect the recent Sharpe to be lower than in-sample, one reason the recent-window test carries a placebo requirement.
limitations: Stock characteristics, not ETF calendar rules; the JF 2016 version reports larger declines (58% post-publication in its abstract as summarized by search).
independent_replication: Peer-reviewed as JF 2016; widely cited, replication of decay in later anomaly studies.
impact_on_spec: Context for decay/placebo/combination design; no parameter chosen from results.
